transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

My mood has been all over the place and I feel constantly revved up and on edge, like I can’t shut myself off. It's like this intense, anxious energy inside me all the time and I'm just so overwhelmed.
When you feel this intense, revved-up energy, do you also experience feelings of deep sadness, hopelessness, or a loss of interest in things at the same time?

Yes, I swing back and forth constantly; I can go from having that wired, angry energy to suddenly crying because I feel so hopeless. I've also completely lost interest in everything I used to love, like my hiking club and planning business ideas, and it feels like there's just no point to any of it anymore.
Do these rapid shifts in your mood usually happen out of the blue, or are they typically triggered by conflicts or changes in your relationships with others?

They are definitely triggered by conflicts with my family, especially lately. My parents have been pushing me to move back home to help care for an ailing relative, and the constant arguments and feeling unsupported really set off these swings. That pressure is what makes me go from feeling wired and snapping to suddenly crying and crashing.
Have these intense mood shifts and sensitivity to conflicts been a constant pattern for you since your teenage years, or do they come in distinct episodes with periods of normal mood in between?

No, this isn't a lifelong pattern from when I was a teenager; it feels like distinct, overwhelming episodes. The intense, revved-up feeling and mood swings started about a month ago when the family pressure began, though I've had periods of heavy depression coming and going for the last four months.

During these periods when you feel so wired and revved up, do you find that you can get by on very little sleep without feeling tired, or are you actually exhausted but unable to sleep because of worry?

I am actually completely exhausted and wiped out, not refreshed at all. My mind is buzzing and racing so much that I just can't sleep, and my body feels like a motor that won't shut off, leaving me shaking from tiredness and feeling like I've run a marathon.

Apart from this current difficult period, have you ever had times in your life lasting at least a few days where you felt unusually happy, extremely confident, and full of energy, needing very little sleep?
No, I've never really experienced anything like this before this past month. This level of extreme energy and these intense mood swings are completely new to me.
When your mind is racing and you can't sleep, are you overwhelmed by constant worries about many different everyday things, or does it feel like your thoughts are just moving too fast to control?

It definitely feels like my thoughts are moving way too fast to control and just crashing into each other, rather than normal worrying. My mind jumps rapidly from things like my uncle's medical bills, to planning a new store layout at work, to random memories from high school. This constant buzzing in my brain is exactly what keeps me from falling asleep.
During these times when your mind is racing, have others commented that you are talking much faster than usual, or do you feel an urgent pressure to keep talking?

Yes, people at work and at home keep telling me to slow down because I talk so fast, especially when I get going on my ideas to fix my family's money issues. I feel this intense physical pressure in my chest that makes it feel almost impossible to stop talking or even pause to take a breath.
Before this past four-month period, have you ever had any other times in your life where you felt deeply depressed, sad, or hopeless for weeks at a time?
No, I haven't really felt this way before this recent period. I don't recall ever having such deep periods of depression prior to these past four months.
During these intense crying spells or when you feel completely hopeless, have you had any thoughts of ending your life or hurting yourself?

Yes, lately I catch myself thinking it would be easier if I just didn't wake up, and on my worst days I've even imagined walking out into traffic after my shift. It's not because I actively want to die, but I just feel so trapped and genuinely believe everyone would be better off without me.

Sometimes these 'high' periods don't feel like happiness, but instead show up as extreme irritability, taking on too many projects, or making impulsive decisions. Have you ever had a period like that in your past, even for just a few days?

Yes, that describes exactly what I have been experiencing over the past month. I've had this wired, angry energy and keep snapping at everyone, while running around nonstop taking on extra shifts and cleaning my apartment at 2 a.m. I've even been trying to start a family business to solve our money problems because I just can't make myself slow down.

During these past four months, did you have times where you felt completely back to your normal self for weeks at a time, or has it felt like one continuous struggle that just changed form a month ago?

Over those first few months, the heavy, depressed feelings were just coming and going rather than being constant. But once the family pressure started a month ago, it became one continuous, intense struggle where my mood completely changed form. Since then, I've been constantly revved up and swinging wildly, and I haven't been able to get back to my normal self at all.

Between the depressive feelings in the first three months and the revved-up feelings that started a month ago, did you have a period of at least a few weeks where your mood returned completely to normal?

I'm not really sure, because my moods have felt so chaotic and blurred together over the last few months. It's really hard to pinpoint if there was a truly normal period in between all of this. It all just feels like a big, confusing mess.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a one-month history of concurrent and rapidly alternating manic and depressive symptoms, including irritable/wired energy, racing thoughts, pressured speech, and increased goal-directed activity, alongside deep sadness, crying spells, loss of interest, and suicidal ideation. This clinical picture is characteristic of a mixed affective episode. Because this is the patient's first mood episode with no prior history of distinct manic, hypomanic, or depressive episodes, it is classified as a single mixed affective disorder under ICD-10 F38.0.
